system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2177-05-05 14:27:00 to 2177-05-08 13:56:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of psoriatic arthritis, chronic steroid use, bilateral corneal transplants, and multiple comorbidities was admitted following sudden onset of right retro-orbital headache and right eye vision changes, including red desaturation and blurriness, after a brief loss of consciousness. Initial evaluation at an eye specialty center prompted transfer for further neurological assessment. Imaging including CT head, MRI brain and orbits, and MRA of head and neck showed no acute intracranial abnormality, mass, or vascular dissection. Laboratory studies were stable, with normal renal function and potassium. The clinical picture was most consistent with right optic neuritis, likely related to his underlying autoimmune condition. Pain was managed conservatively, and no changes were made to his chronic medications, including dexamethasone and azathioprine. He was discharged home with instructions to follow up with neurology and ophthalmology, to start outpatient terbinafine for a fungal infection, and to monitor for worsening symptoms. Pending blood tests include fungal cultures, RPR, and ACE levels.
problems: Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___ from the medicine team. I understand you came in after feeling very lightheaded at home yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. My wife took my blood pressure and it was really low—56 over 48. I couldn’t stand up without getting dizzy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s quite low. I see you also had some visual hallucinations this morning—seeing animals and strange writing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was very vivid. I knew it wasn’t real, but it felt real at the time. I’ve had episodes like this before when my blood pressure drops.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Given your history of chronic steroid use for psoriatic arthritis, we’re concerned this was an adrenal crisis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Adrenal crisis? I’ve heard of that. Is that why I felt so weak and had low blood pressure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your body relies on steroids because your adrenal glands don’t make enough on their own. When you’re under stress—even from something like a new medication—it can trigger a crisis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did get my first dose of rituximab two days ago. Could that have caused this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible. Rituximab can be a stress on the body. We don’t think you had an infection—your chest X-ray was clear, and blood cultures show no growth so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. But my kidneys—are they okay? I’ve had issues before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine was elevated at 1.8 when you arrived, but that’s likely due to the low blood pressure. It’s already improving with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not permanent damage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, this looks like acute kidney injury from poor perfusion. As your blood pressure stabilizes, your kidneys should return to normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I also had brief chest pressure in the ER—nothing like my usual chest wall pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we noted that. It was brief and didn’t change with movement. Your EKG was stable, and troponins were normal, so we don’t think it was a heart issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. What about my medications? I take a lot of them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve continued your dexamethasone and insulin. We held your carvedilol and lisinopril temporarily because they can lower blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. Should I stop any of them permanently?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re stopping nortriptyline for now. It can contribute to hallucinations and worsen orthostatic hypotension.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on that for nerve pain. Is it safe to stop?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor you. If the neuropathy flares, your primary doctor can consider alternatives that are safer for you now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are improving. Creatinine is down to 1.2, and your blood pressure is stable at 128 over 64.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. No more hallucinations, and I feel much stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’re going to restart your carvedilol today at a lower dose and monitor you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I take extra steroids before my next rituximab infusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your rheumatologist may recommend a stress dose of hydrocortisone during future infusions. An overnight observation stay might also be wise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds like a good plan. I don’t want to go through this again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are nearly back to baseline. Creatinine is 1.1, and your mental status is completely clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m feeling like myself again. Can I go home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if your blood pressure stays stable through the day, we’ll discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any dizziness, confusion, nausea, or vomiting—especially if you can’t keep fluids down. Those could be signs of another adrenal issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I get sick—like a cold or flu—should I adjust my steroids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You should double your dexamethasone for three days if you have a fever or infection. We’ll give you a steroid action plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your endocrinologist and rheumatologist next week. They’ll discuss pretreatment planning for future rituximab doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge. Your blood pressure is stable, labs are good, and you’re walking without dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. So I continue all my meds except nortriptyline?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. And remember—stress dose steroids if you get sick, and talk to your doctor before restarting nortriptyline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you for taking such good care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of psoriatic arthritis on chronic steroids was admitted after experiencing hypotension, visual hallucinations, and acute kidney injury at home, one day after receiving his first rituximab infusion. He was found to have an adrenal crisis, likely triggered by the physiological stress of the new biologic therapy. He received intravenous hydrocortisone and fluids in the emergency department with rapid improvement in blood pressure and mental status. His renal function normalized within 24 hours. Nortriptyline was discontinued due to its potential to worsen hallucinations and orthostatic hypotension. His home medications, including dexamethasone and insulin, were continued, and antihypertensives were restarted prior to discharge. He was discharged home in stable condition with plans to coordinate stress-dose steroid coverage and possible observation for future rituximab infusions with his specialists.
